source.title: SAGE: Scalable Ground Truth Evaluations for Large Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Constantin Venhoff; A. Calinescu; P. Torr; Christian Schroeder de Witt

record.tranche_reason: The study compares SAE feature dictionaries with supervised task-specific feature dictionaries using reconstruction, necessity, and feature-editing evaluations in language models. These evaluations bear on SAE recovery of task features, but do not reproduce toy-model superposition experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper cites toy-model superposition work in related work but reports no new toy-network superposition results. Hyperparameters and cross-section selection values are not recorded as findings. Exact plotted SAE scores are not stated in the text; rows retain figure-only values where applicable.
record.test_reason: The paper's aim is a framework (SAGE), but it reports measured sufficiency, necessity and sparse-control results for open-source residual SAEs on GPT-2 Small, Pythia 70M and Gemma-2-2B. These are compared with supervised task-feature dictionaries. The results bear on how well SAEs recover and control real task features (V4) and whether SAE features act as complete units (V5). The evidence is weakened by two choices: the reference is only approximate ground truth, and SAE features are applied through the authors' new projection-based reconstruction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' stated conclusion is about the framework: SAGE scales ground-truth SAE evaluation to new tasks and models (up to Gemma-2-2B) using only residual-stream SAEs, and finds high-quality supervised dictionaries. The finding that SAEs underperform supervised dictionaries, with larger SAEs doing better, is reported in the results rather than emphasised as a conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates residual-stream SAEs against supervised task-feature dictionaries using sufficiency, necessity, and sparse-control tests. It does not use the original toy-model superposition setup or its sparsity and geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with SAE dictionary size, task, model, and induction cross-section group; the text reports different effects of additional edits across groups.
record.problems: The SAE numerical scores are presented in figures without exact values in the text. The ground-truth dictionaries are described as approximate. The authors note that cross-section discovery depends on attribution patching and may be constrained by its effectiveness.
record.rows_left_out: Individual plotted SAE scores and detailed per-group values from Figures 2 and 3 are not transcribed where the text does not state them; rows record the textual comparisons and selected explicitly stated induction edit rates.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy networks, sparsity sweeps or geometry.
All of it: no test of capacity pressure as the cause of polysemanticity.
All of it: no alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Whether features are spread across many neurons; recovery is tested only for a few task attributes (names, order).
Stability across SAE training runs and canonicity; completeness is probed only for narrow task attributes.
All of it: feature dimensionality is not examined.

missing.what: Induction-task results on GPT-2 Small with animal, country and number feature distributions (Test 1 and Test 2).
missing.versions: V4, V5 (figure only, no text values)

missing.what: IOI subject-increase SAE/supervised edits flip the prediction to a general token ('the') rather than the target.
Supervised-dictionary scores, as reference rows: sufficiency/necessity >0.95 (IOI) and >0.9 (induction); edit success >90% (IOI) and >80% (induction).

record.verdict_notes: Borderline T4: the SAE comparisons serve mainly to validate the framework. SAE results depend on the novel alignment-filter reconstruction, which is not separately validated. The supervised dictionaries are approximate ground truth. No uncertainty is reported, and most SAE values are figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-over-dimension sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, or superposition geometry are tested.
The study does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
No alternative causes of polysemanticity are tested.
The study evaluates SAE recovery and control of task-specific features, but does not measure whether features are spread across many neurons.
The study evaluates SAE reconstruction and control against approximate supervised task features, but does not test feature stability across runs or whether SAE features are canonical units.
The dimensionality or geometry of individual features is not tested.

rows.measure: Sparse controllability / influence on model predictions
rows.baseline: Supervised feature dictionary: over 90% edit success across all cross-section groups
rows.value: The SAE struggles; even 16 feature edits fail to significantly influence predictions in the subject and order groups
rows.note: The study also reports that edits in the subject-increase group can cause prediction flips, including to a general token such as “the,” rather than the intended target.
rows.check: For the subject and order groups, the text says 16 edits 'fail to significantly influence' predictions. That is no effect beyond baseline, so the state is absent, not partial. The 32k SAE 'does not improve' in any group.

relation.reason: The paper reports its own reconstruction and intervention evaluations of SAE dictionaries against supervised task-feature dictionaries.

tranche.reason: The relevant results show incomplete task-feature reconstruction and failed control in specified settings, qualifying V5's complete-unit account; this matches the supplied T5 definition.

source_check.notes: Supervised dictionaries approximate task ground truth; SAE results depend on projection-based sublayer reconstruction and greedy sparse editing. These experiments do not directly test dictionary stability or canonicity.

statements.problem: The SAGE result is accurately reported, but failed sparse control alone does not limit V4's claim that dictionaries can recover sparse features.
